tldr: A whole-body residual control framework that estimates contact forces and cart motion latents purely from proprioception and a head camera—without external force sensors or human demonstrations—enabling accurate and smooth pushing of carts loaded up to 30 kg using reinforcement learning.
hero_caption: The overall ForPC framework: (a) a locomotion prior pre-trained under randomized disturbance wrenches on the hands, (b) a Teacher-Student latent estimator that infers privileged contact wrenches and cart motion states from onboard signals, and (c) a residual policy that takes these latents to produce joint residuals across the upper and lower body alongside base velocity commands.
overview:
When humanoid robots transport heavy loads in manufacturing or logistics, operating existing wheeled carts designed for humans allows them to shoulder strenuous material handling without modifying infrastructure. However, walking while bimanually grasping a cart handle creates a closed force-coupled loop: the contact wrenches that propel the cart also act as disturbances upsetting the robot's balance, and payload variations drastically shift the coupled dynamics. Furthermore, poor coordination between the arms leads to internal opposition, where the hands fight each other and waste actuator torque.

To solve this, the authors propose ForPC, a force-aware whole-body control framework using two-stage reinforcement learning. In the first stage, a robust locomotion prior is pre-trained and frozen under severe, randomized hand wrenches and varied upper-body postures. In the second stage, an inference module estimates contact force and cart motion as latent representations using only onboard sensors (joint positions, velocities, upper-body torques) and the cart's relative orientation from a head camera. Conditioned on these latents, a residual policy coordinates base velocity command adjustments with arm, waist, and leg joint offsets, regulating cart velocity through coordinated whole-body actions.

In Isaac Sim evaluations, ForPC reduced cart-velocity root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 68.2% and cross-track error on a multi-bend route by up to 74.2% compared to a locomotion-only baseline (Loco-only). Furthermore, the policy trained purely in simulation was transferred zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1 robot, stably pushing a cart loaded with up to 30 kg at 0.5 m/s with no real-world fine-tuning or payload-specific adjustments.
contributions: Proposed ForPC, a two-stage reinforcement learning framework combining a locomotion prior, an interaction inference module, and a whole-body residual policy for dynamic cart pushing.

Constructed a force-guided inference module that estimates force and motion latents from onboard signals without external force sensors, closing both contact-load and cart-behavior feedback loops simultaneously.
Designed a multi-objective reward function that penalizes bimanual internal opposition, efficiently directing contact forces into effective cart propulsion.
Transferred a single sim-trained policy zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1, achieving route-following transport of carts carrying up to 30 kg without parameter tuning.

sections.heading: Why is cart pushing so difficult for humanoids?
sections.summary: When a humanoid pushes a wheeled cart, bimanual grasping creates a force-coupled loop that introduces a trade-off between balance maintenance and propulsion control. Existing methods only estimate either forces or motion, failing to address internal opposition between the arms. This paper presents ForPC, a force-aware whole-body control framework that tackles both challenges simultaneously.
sections.details:
Having humanoids autonomously operate manual handcarts designed for people could greatly streamline heavy material handling in logistics and manufacturing. In practice, however, this task faces severe dynamic coupling challenges.

First, grasping the cart handle with both hands turns the robot and the cart into a single, tightly coupled dynamic system. Pushing the cart forward produces an equal and opposite reaction wrench straight into the robot's upper body, disturbing its walking balance. Furthermore, variations in payload mass and center of mass drastically alter how the cart responds to applied forces. Another critical issue is bimanual internal opposition: because both hands grasp a single rigid handle, poor coordination causes one arm to push against the other. This internal force contributes nothing to moving the cart forward, needlessly draining actuator torque margins needed for balance correction and steering.

While wrist force/torque sensors can measure contact forces, not every robot has them, and carts in the field are typically uninstrumented. Prior studies attempted to infer external forces or object motions from proprioception (such as joint angles and torques), but none closed the loop by simultaneously feeding back both cart velocity and bimanual contact wrenches. To overcome this, the authors developed ForPC, which infers both contact force and motion states as latent variables using onboard signals alone, orchestrating walking and bimanual manipulation across the entire body.

sections.heading: Current landscape of cart pushing, force-adaptive control, and residual RL
sections.summary: Humanoid transport control has transitioned from model-based methods to reinforcement learning, substantially increasing manageable payloads. However, coordinating whole-body actions by simultaneously estimating contact wrenches and object motion remained unaddressed. Furthermore, existing residual RL approaches have focused on motion tracking or disturbance rejection, making them ill-suited for driving uninstrumented mobile objects.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Humanoid Cart Pushing and Object Transport
Early studies attempted dual-arm force control or simultaneous planning of the center of mass and contact wrenches based on cart models, but these relied on precise object dynamics and external force sensors. Recently, reinforcement learning has substantially increased pushable payloads—such as pushing carts exceeding 100 kg or predicting object motion from proprioception (e.g., HAIC). However, because required contact forces change with payload mass and distribution, an online framework that simultaneously estimates and leverages both hand wrenches and cart motion remained missing.

### 2.2 Force Estimation and Force-Adaptive Control
To incorporate contact forces into control loops, approaches like FACET (which uses virtual spring-damper systems) and proprioceptive force estimation techniques developed on legged robots (e.g., quadruped manipulator work by Portela et al., CompliantWBC) have been adapted to humanoids. Nonetheless, these frameworks primarily aim to track target forces or compliantly absorb external disturbances, rather than tracking how the manipulated object moves in response.

### 2.3 Residual Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Control
Instead of training whole-body locomotion from scratch, residual reinforcement learning (Residual RL)—which adds task-specific corrections on top of an existing locomotion controller—has gained traction. Existing works include motion capture tracking corrections (ResMimic) and cancelling hand or tray vibrations (SEEC, SteadyTray). However, these policies focus on stabilizing target states and cannot be directly applied to driving carts with unknown dynamics toward commanded velocities.

sections.heading: Decoupling cart pushing into two distinct subsystems
sections.summary: In the coupled robot-cart system, unknown payloads, hand forces, and cart velocities form unobserved states. Learning locomotion and transport simultaneously in a single policy leads to intractable exploration. Therefore, the problem is formulated into two stages: learning locomotion under disturbances (Subsystem 1) and controlling the cart via an interaction estimator (Subsystem 2).
sections.details:
Consider a robot grasping the handle of a caster-wheeled cart to track a commanded planar cart velocity $\bm{v}^{\mathrm{cart,cmd}}_{t}$.

The system state is divided into an observable state $\bm{s}^{\mathrm{obs}}_{t}$ obtained directly from onboard sensors and cameras, and an unobservable state $\bm{s}^{\mathrm{unobs}}_{t}$ comprising hand contact wrenches $\bm{F}^{\mathrm{hand}}_{t}$, actual cart velocity $\bm{v}^{\mathrm{cart}}_{t}$, and unknown payload mass. Because a four-caster cart has no directional constraints from fixed wheels, lateral translation and steering must be guided almost entirely by hand wrenches and torques, making unobserved dynamic information essential.

However, training locomotion and cart manipulation from scratch in a single stage fails because the vast unobserved state space overwhelms RL exploration. The authors cleanly separated the physically coupled system into two reinforcement learning stages:

- **Subsystem 1 (Locomotion Stabilization)**: The cart is omitted entirely. Instead, reaction wrenches from the cart are applied to the robot's hands as randomized external forces and disturbance moments $\bm{F}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{t}$. Here, a robust locomotion prior $\pi_{\mathrm{base}}$ is trained to maintain commanded walking velocities without falling, regardless of pushing or pulling disturbances.
- **Subsystem 2 (Cart Velocity Control)**: The locomotion prior is frozen, and the cart is physically connected. The unobserved state $\bm{s}^{\mathrm{unobs}}_{t}$ is reconstructed as latent representations from joint motion and torque histories $\bm{H}_{t}$ via an estimator $\mathcal{E}$. A task policy $\pi_{\mathrm{task}}$ then outputs residual actions $\bm{a}^{\mathrm{res}}_{t}$ over the locomotion prior to steer the cart accurately.

sections.heading: Designing ForPC: locomotion prior, latent estimation, and whole-body residual coordination
sections.summary: ForPC consists of three core components: (1) pre-training a locomotion prior resilient to hand disturbances, (2) a Teacher-Student estimator that infers motion states guided by contact force latents, and (3) a task policy that outputs base velocity commands and joint residuals across the upper and lower body while suppressing bimanual internal opposition.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Locomotion Prior for Interactive Cart Pushing
In the first stage, a walking controller $\pi_{\mathrm{base}}$ is trained to withstand reaction wrenches and posture variations encountered during cart pushing. In simulation, 3-axis external forces and moments are randomly injected into the robot's palms, while arm and waist joint targets are perturbed within bounded ranges. The reward function encourages base velocity tracking, trunk height and orientation stability, foot clearance and slip prevention, alongside regularization terms against excessive joint torques and abrupt motions. Once trained, this network's weights are frozen.

### 4.2 Latent Interaction Dynamics Inference Under Partial Observability
The cornerstone of the second stage is inferring contact forces and cart motion without external force sensors. The authors adopt a distillation setup with a Teacher (which accesses privileged simulation states like ground-truth contact wrenches and cart velocities) and a Student (which only takes real-world observation histories $\bm{H}_{t}$, including joint positions/velocities, upper-body torques, and the cart's relative yaw from the camera).

A key architectural innovation is the force-guided design: a causal temporal encoder first infers a force latent $\hat{\bm{z}}^{F}_{t}$ from observation histories, and this force latent sequence is then fused with observation features to infer the state latent $\hat{\bm{z}}^{s}_{t}$. In essence, the network estimates cart motion by conditioning on its awareness of applied contact forces. Auxiliary reconstruction tasks for contact wrenches, as well as cart and base velocities and accelerations, are trained jointly to ground the latent space in physical dynamics.

### 4.3 Force-Aware Whole-Body Residual Coordinated Control
The task policy $\pi_{\mathrm{task}}$ receives the estimated force and state latents alongside recent observations to output a 30-dimensional residual action: base velocity adjustments to the locomotion prior (3D), arm and waist joint residuals (15D), and leg joint residuals (12D). This coordinates walking gaits, upper-body force exertion, and lower-body stance under a single policy.

Crucially, the reward function addresses dual-arm coordination. When both hands grasp a single handle, the hand wrench $\bm{F}^{\mathrm{hand}}_{t}$ can be orthogonally decomposed into a driving component $\bm{d}^{\mathrm{dr}}_{t}$ that accelerates the cart, and an internal component $\bm{d}^{\mathrm{int}}_{t}$ where the two hands cancel each other out. By penalizing this internal wrench component in the reward, the policy autonomously learns to avoid fighting itself, directing actuator torque efficiently into forward motion and turning.

captions.F2: The overall pipeline of the method: (a) pre-training a robust locomotion prior under hand disturbance wrenches, (b) inferring force and state latents from onboard signals via Teacher-Student distillation, and (c) optimizing whole-body coordination through a frozen locomotion prior and a learnable residual policy guided by internal force penalties.

sections.heading: Simulation evaluations and physical Unitree G1 validation
sections.summary: Comparative experiments in Isaac Sim and MuJoCo confirmed that ForPC reduces velocity tracking RMSE by up to 68.2%, cuts cross-track error by up to 74.2%, and substantially suppresses bimanual internal opposition. Furthermore, the sim-trained policy transferred directly to a physical Unitree G1, stably pushing a 30 kg payload at 0.5 m/s.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup
The robot used is a Unitree G1 featuring 12 leg DOFs, a 1-DOF waist yaw, and 14 arm DOFs, operating a four-caster cart (12 kg tare mass). An AprilTag on the cart's top plate is tracked by a head RealSense camera to capture relative yaw. Training is conducted in Isaac Sim at a 50 Hz control frequency. Baseline comparisons include: (1) Loco-only (pushing with the locomotion prior without residual task corrections), (2) a variant using a locomotion prior pre-trained without hand disturbances, and (3) a force-unaware variant omitting force latent estimation. Sim-to-sim generalization was also validated in MuJoCo, which features different contact dynamics.

### 5.2 Cart Pushing Performance (Velocity and Path Tracking)
In velocity tracking evaluations, step commands were given for forward travel (0.3, 0.5, 0.8 m/s), lateral translation (0.15, 0.3 m/s), and steering (0.15, 0.3 rad/s). As shown in Figure F3, while Loco-only tracked forward commands, it failed on lateral and turning maneuvers due to rolling resistance. In contrast, ForPC rapidly tracked commands across all directions. In Table 1, ForPC reduced velocity tracking RMSE by up to 68.2% and velocity fluctuation (RMSF) by up to 65.4% compared to Loco-only. Incorporating force awareness specifically improved lateral tracking error by up to 36.1%.

On a multi-bend route involving S-curves and right-angle detours (Figure F4), ForPC reduced cross-track RMSE by up to 74.2%, achieving a 100% success rate under both 15 kg and 25 kg payload conditions (Table 2). The robot maintained balance and tracked the path smoothly even under heavy loads and sharp turns.

### 5.3 Latent Representation Analysis and Bimanual Coordination
Evaluating the Student estimator revealed a coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of 0.97 along the forward axis and 0.95 along the vertical axis for 3-axis palm contact forces. Cart velocity estimation RMSE reached an accurate 0.035 m/s. Furthermore, measuring the internal force ratio $\rho^{\mathrm{int}}$ (Table 4) showed that while the force-unaware baseline exhibited high internal opposition that wasted torque, ForPC lowered the internal force ratio by up to 34.6 percentage points, efficiently concentrating horizontal effort into cart propulsion.

### 5.4 Deployment on the Physical Unitree G1
The policy trained in simulation was transferred zero-shot to the physical Unitree G1 without any real-world fine-tuning. As shown in Figure F5, the robot reliably performed forward pushing, lateral stepping, and in-place pivoting on flat ground. Integrated with an onboard navigation system, the robot traversed narrow corridors, paused at a transfer station where an operator changed the payload, and transported payloads of varying weights (up to 30 kg) to the destination at 0.5 m/s using a single policy without parameter changes (Figure F6).

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: ForPC demonstrates highly precise humanoid cart pushing through force-aware whole-body residual control. By inferring contact wrenches and motion states without external sensors and curbing bimanual internal opposition, the framework achieves zero-shot physical deployment with a 30 kg payload. Future directions include extending to diverse wheeled equipment and integrating vision for cluttered environments.
sections.details:
This paper presented ForPC, a novel whole-body control framework enabling humanoid robots to push wheeled carts with high precision.

By uniting three key elements—a locomotion prior pre-trained under disturbance wrenches, a force-guided inference module reconstructing contact wrenches and cart motion from onboard signals, and a residual policy coordinating base commands and whole-body joint offsets while penalizing bimanual fighting—the system realizes robust transport control without external force sensors or prior payload calibration. In addition to dramatic accuracy gains in simulation, the zero-shot physical deployment on the Unitree G1 moving a 30 kg payload highlights the realistic potential of humanoids taking over everyday material handling.

For future work, the authors plan to extend the framework to various wheeled devices (such as hospital beds and wheelchairs), support alternate grasp modes, and incorporate exteroceptive perception (vision and LiDAR) for maneuvering through cluttered environments.

takeaways: Decoupling the problem into locomotion stabilization (disturbance-robust pre-training) and cart manipulation (residual learning) substantially improves RL exploration in strongly coupled contact tasks.
Even without wrist force sensors, contact wrenches and object motion can be accurately reconstructed as latent representations from joint motion and torque histories.

In bimanual tasks, decomposing contact wrenches into driving and internal components to penalize internal opposition is key to preventing arms from fighting each other and maximizing torque efficiency.
limitations: The hand grasp posture is fixed; dynamic regrasping, single-handed pushing, and adapting to varied handle geometries were not evaluated.
Cart relative yaw estimation relies on an AprilTag detected by a head camera, leaving robustness unverified in markerless or occluded environments.
The maximum tested payload was 30 kg (42 kg including cart tare mass); pushing and pulling ultra-heavy loads exceeding human body weight requires further investigation.
